questions.q: Which of the following histopathological features is most helpful in distinguishing trichoepithelioma from basal cell carcinoma?
opts: Presence of basaloid cells with peripheral palisading
Presence of cribriform pattern within lobules
Tight adherence of stroma to follicular germinative cells with clefts lacking retraction artifact
Small cornifying cystic spaces with surrounding keratinocytes
questions.exp: Trichoepithelioma maintains tightly adherent contact between the fibrocytic stroma and follicular germinative cells with clefts that lack retraction artifact. This distinguishes it from basal cell carcinoma, which typically shows retraction artifact around the stromal-epithelial interface. Both lesions may share basaloid morphology and palisading, but the stromal relationship is the key differentiator.

questions.q: A 12-year-old child with Kindler Syndrome, who presented with acral blistering and severe photosensitivity as an infant, now presents with progressive poikiloderma, widespread cutaneous atrophy, and characteristic 'cigarette paper-like' skin on the dorsal hands. At what developmental stage does this distinctive phenotypic shift typically occur?
opts: Within the first 3 months of life
By approximately age 8 years
During adolescence (age 13–16 years)
In early adulthood after age 20 years
questions.exp: Kindler Syndrome exhibits a dynamic clinical evolution: the neonatal/infancy phase features trauma-induced acral blistering and photosensitivity, but paradoxically, these tendencies improve as the child ages. By approximately age 8 years, patients typically transition to the characteristic poikilodermatous phase with progressive, lifelong poikiloderma, widespread cutaneous atrophy, and the pathognomonic 'cigarette paper-like' atrophy of acral surfaces.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: At age 8, the castle's BLISTERS SEAL UP like closing gates, but the TAPESTRIES FADE AND SHRIVEL (poikiloderma and atrophy emerge)—the child's skin transforms from angry and fragile to wrinkled and thin, like old parchment burning at the edges.

questions.q: A 32-year-old patient with a family history of lupus develops annular polycyclic lesions on sun-exposed areas. Genetic testing reveals heterozygous TREX1 gene mutations. Which form of chronic cutaneous lupus erythematosus is this patient at highest risk of developing?
opts: Hypertrophic discoid lupus erythematosus
Chilblain lupus erythematosus
Mucosal discoid lupus erythematosus
Lichenoid lupus erythematosus
questions.exp: Heterozygous mutations in the TREX1 gene are specifically identified as the underlying genetic cause of familial chilblain lupus (CHLE). Chilblain LE is classified as a form of Chronic Cutaneous Lupus Erythematosus (CCLE) and typically presents with lesions on acral areas following cold exposure. The TREX1 gene mutation is a well-established genetic marker for this specific phenotype.
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: In the frozen CHILBLAIN CHAMBER of the castle, the TREX1 GUARD (imagine a shivering sentinel with icy hands) protects the ACRAL GATE. When the guard's defenses are weakened by heterozygous TREX1 mutations, cold-triggered CHILBLAIN lesions breach the castle during winter—TREX1 = TRENCH-FOOT EXTREMITY 1.

questions.q: A 6-month-old infant presents with recurrent blistering on the dorsal surfaces of the hands and feet following minor trauma, along with severe photosensitivity. Genetic testing reveals homozygous loss-of-function mutations in the FERMT1 gene. Which of the following best describes the pathophysiological basis of this condition?
opts: Autoimmune-mediated loss of desmogleins with circulating pathogenic autoantibodies
Deficiency of kindlin-1, a focal adhesion protein linking actin filaments to the extracellular matrix
Type VII collagen mutations in the sub-basal lamina region
HLA-associated immune complex deposition at the dermoepidermal junction
questions.exp: Kindler Syndrome results from loss-of-function mutations in FERMT1 gene encoding kindlin-1, a critical focal adhesion protein that links actin filaments within basal keratinocytes to the underlying extracellular matrix. This is a primary structural genetic disorder, not an autoimmune condition, so autoimmune serology and HLA associations are absent. The pathogenesis involves impaired keratinocyte adhesion, shape, polarity, and motility.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Picture a FERRIS WHEEL (FERMT1) in the castle that WEAVES GOLDEN THREADS (kindlin-1 linking actin to matrix) through the stone walls—without it, the walls crumble at the foundation when knights (trauma) attack.

questions.q: A 2-week-old female neonate presents with linear, punctate atrophic lesions on the trunk and extremities that follow a specific anatomical distribution pattern. Genetic testing reveals a loss-of-function mutation in the PORCN gene on chromosome Xp11.23. Which of the following best explains why approximately 90% of patients with Focal Dermal Hypoplasia are female?
opts: Females have two X chromosomes, allowing for functional mosaicism through random X-inactivation, whereas hemizygous males with the mutation typically die in utero
The PORCN gene is only expressed in females, making males immune to the pathological effects of the mutation
Females are more likely to inherit X-linked dominant conditions from affected mothers, while affected males cannot pass the condition to sons
Female hormones provide protective effects against the pathogenic consequences of PORCN mutations during embryonic development
questions.exp: FDH is an X-linked dominant disorder caused by PORCN mutations. The non-mosaic hemizygous form is lethal in males during intrauterine development. Surviving females benefit from random X-chromosome inactivation (lyonization), which creates functional mosaicism with a mixture of normal and mutant cells distributed along the lines of Blaschko. Surviving males (~10% of cases) must have either somatic mosaicism from a late post-zygotic mutation or Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY).
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: Picture 90% of the royal female guards standing in two X-shaped armor formations in the castle hall—ONE guard dies in the single-X male guards' barracks. The females survive because BOTH X's allow mixed-mosaic shields; males with only ONE faulty X don't make it past the castle gates.

questions.q: A 6-month-old boy presents with multiple pink-red macules with subtle blanched halos scattered across his arms and trunk. Doppler ultrasound confirms normal flow velocity. Genetic testing reveals a RASA1 mutation. Which ISSVA classification category best describes this vascular anomaly?
opts: Vascular tumour with fast-flow dynamics requiring urgent imaging
Simple, slow-flow capillary malformation existing as an isolated anomaly
Combined malformation of major named vessels with arteriovenous involvement
Associated vascular malformation as a hallmark feature of Sturge-Weber syndrome
questions.exp: This clinical presentation—multiple capillary malformations with RASA1 mutation, blanched halos, and normal (slow) flow on Doppler—represents capillary malformation-arteriovenous malformation (CM-AVM) spectrum. Capillary malformations are classified as simple, slow-flow malformations composed of a single dysplastic vessel type (capillary bed). RASA1 mutations are the genetic hallmark of this condition.
questions.source: [Paeds Day 2] ISSVA Classification and Capillary Malformations
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: A RASA1 CASTLE brick has a PINK halo (blanched rim = CM trademark) floating SLOWLY through the moat—simple, single-vessel malformation, not tumour; not fast-flow.

questions.q: Kennedy and Pottier's 1990 breakthrough discovery regarding 5-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) made PDT practical for routine dermatologic use primarily because:
opts: ALA is a topical prodrug that induces localized intracutaneous production of protoporphyrin IX, avoiding systemic photosensitivity complications
ALA can be administered intravenously with a shorter photosensitivity period of 2–3 weeks
ALA produces hematoporphyrin derivative that fluoresces under Wood's lamp at 595 nm
ALA eliminates the need for external light sources during treatment of acne vulgaris
questions.exp: Kennedy and Pottier's discovery that topical ALA could induce localized production of the active photosensitizer protoporphyrin IX (PpIX) was revolutionary because it bypassed the severe limitations of earlier systemic photosensitizers like porfimer sodium, which caused generalized cutaneous photosensitivity lasting 6–8 weeks. The topical prodrug approach restricted photosensitization to the target tissue, making PDT practical for routine dermatologic use.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: In the castle's apothecary, a MAGIC POTION (ALA) is poured onto the SKIN WALL, transforming into GLOWING PURPLE POWDER (PpIX) only within the bricks—the rest of the castle remains dark and safe from sunlight.

questions.q: Histopathological examination of a skin biopsy from a child with Gianotti-Crosti syndrome shows epidermal spongiosis, mild acanthosis, parakeratosis, and a patchy perivascular lymphohistiocytic infiltrate in the superficial dermis. Which of the following additional clinical or investigative findings would MOST reliably distinguish the classic HBV-associated form from the non-HBV papulovesicular variant?
opts: Presence of marked epidermal spongiosis and substantially more pronounced dermal inflammation on histology
Detection of Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) in serum combined with signs of acute anicteric hepatitis
Increased pruritus, vesicular morphology, and longer disease duration
Age of presentation under 4 years and involvement of palms and soles
questions.exp: Classic Gianotti-Crosti syndrome is specifically defined by concurrent Hepatitis B surface antigen positivity and acute anicteric hepatitis. While both forms share similar basal histological features (spongiosis and perivascular inflammation), only the HBV-associated variant includes systemic hepatic involvement. The non-HBV form is distinguished by increased pruritus and vesicularity rather than hepatic disease.

questions.q: Which three fundamental components must be present simultaneously within target tissue for photodynamic therapy to be effective?
opts: Photosensitizing molecule, photoactivating light wavelengths, and tissue oxygen
Photosensitizing molecule, ultraviolet radiation, and tissue water
Porphyrin derivative, infrared light, and tissue perfusion
Organic dye, visible light spectrum, and tissue pH >7
questions.exp: Photodynamic therapy requires the simultaneous presence of a tissue-localized photosensitizing molecule, photoactivating wavelengths of light, and molecular oxygen to generate the photochemical reaction. The interaction of these three components produces reactive oxygen species, particularly singlet oxygen, which initiates cellular apoptosis and tissue destruction.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Three royal guards stand at the castle gate—the PURPLE PHOTOSENSITIZER holds a LIGHT TORCH while OXYGEN (O₂) floats as mist around them; remove any one guard and the castle gate stays locked.

questions.q: A 2-week-old male presents with a fully formed, protuberant red-violaceous lesion on his leg that was present at birth. Immunohistochemistry shows GLUT1-negative staining. The lesion begins to show signs of regression by 6 weeks of age. Which genetic mutation most likely underlies this congenital haemangioma?
opts: GNAQ/GNA11 Gln209 missense mutation
VEGFR2 activating mutation
PTEN loss-of-function mutation
PIK3CA exon 20 mutation
questions.exp: Congenital haemangiomas are driven by somatic activating missense mutations in GNAQ and GNA11 genes at the Gln209 locus, which constitutively upregulate the MAPK pathway during prenatal growth. This mutation is shared across all three subtypes (RICH, NICH, PICH) and distinguishes congenital haemangiomas from infantile haemangiomas, which are GLUT1-positive and have different molecular drivers.

questions.q: Which of the following characteristics distinguishes vascular malformations from vascular tumours according to the ISSVA classification?
opts: Vascular malformations are true neoplasms driven by endothelial hyperplasia and are GLUT1-positive
Vascular malformations are present at birth, possess quiescent flat endothelium, and are universally GLUT1-negative
Vascular malformations undergo rapid postnatal growth followed by involution over years
Vascular malformations demonstrate elevated PCNA markers and active cellular proliferation
questions.exp: Vascular malformations are morphogenetic errors of embryonic development with dysplastic vessels lined by quiescent endothelium, normal cellular turnover, and absence of GLUT1 expression. In contrast, vascular tumours (such as infantile haemangioma) are true neoplasms with active endothelial proliferation, elevated PCNA, GLUT1-positivity, and a characteristic clinical course of rapid postnatal growth followed by slow involution.
questions.source: [Paeds Day 2] ISSVA Classification and Capillary Malformations
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: Picture a FLAT SLEEPING ENDOTHELIUM on a QUIET castle bed (malformation = quiescent), while a HYPERACTIVE GLUT1 VAMPIRE screams and proliferates in the tower (tumour = GLUT1+, hyper).

questions.q: A 45-year-old patient presents with a suspected melanoma on the dorsal forearm measuring 8 mm. Which biopsy modality is contraindicated and why?
opts: Excisional biopsy, as it produces excessive scarring
Shave biopsy, due to compromise of Breslow depth assessment
Punch biopsy, due to inadequate specimen size
Incisional biopsy, due to incomplete tumor removal
questions.exp: Shave biopsies are contraindicated in suspected melanoma because they sample only the superficial dermis via saucerization, preventing accurate assessment of Breslow depth—a critical prognostic factor. Excisional biopsy is the gold standard for melanoma as it provides complete lesion removal with full margin assessment and accurate depth determination.

questions.q: A patient with suspected pemphigus vulgaris requires a biopsy for direct immunofluorescence (DIF) analysis. Which statement regarding specimen handling is correct?
opts: A single punch biopsy from the center of the blister is adequate, fixed in formalin
A separate perilesional skin biopsy must be obtained and placed in Michel's medium or normal saline, never formalin
An old, healed blister should be sampled to allow adequate re-epithelialization for better visualization
A shave biopsy of the lesional edge provides optimal immunofluorescence results
questions.exp: Direct immunofluorescence requires a separate biopsy of perilesional (not lesional) skin placed in Michel's medium, Zeus medium, or normal saline because formalin destroys the immunoglobulins necessary for diagnostic visualization. Fresh, intact blisters from the lesional edge are used for routine histology, but perilesional skin is essential for DIF to detect tissue-bound antibodies.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman presents with multiple firm, red nodules on her scalp covering a large area. Histopathology reveals lobules of basaloid cells with peripheral palisading, cribriform pattern, and a conspicuous fibrocytic stroma maintaining tightly adherent contact without retraction artifact. Genetic testing shows a mutation in the CYLD gene on chromosome 16. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Basal cell carcinoma with syndromic features
Multiple familial trichoepitheliomas associated with Brooke-Spiegler syndrome
Merkel cell carcinoma with hereditary predisposition
Pilomatricoma with autosomal recessive inheritance
questions.exp: Multiple familial trichoepitheliomas are inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern and are linked to CYLD gene mutations on chromosome 16, often as part of Brooke-Spiegler syndrome. The clinical presentation of multiple scalp lesions ('turban tumour') and the characteristic histopathological findings with basaloid lobules and fibrocytic stroma are classic for trichoepithelioma. The absence of retraction artifact helps distinguish this from basal cell carcinoma.

questions.q: A dermatologist evaluates a 3-month-old girl with a diagnosis of Focal Dermal Hypoplasia. On examination, the child has cribriform (ice pick-like) atrophic patches with visible subcutaneous fat herniation. The lesions demonstrate a linear distribution limited to one side of the body midline. Which layer of the skin is primarily affected in the pathogenesis of this condition?
opts: The epidermis, where mutations in PORCN disrupt melanocyte differentiation and migration
The dermis, where failure of Wnt signaling-mediated connective tissue formation results in profound thinning
The hypodermis and subcutaneous tissue, where loss of adipocyte regulation leads to fat atrophy
The basement membrane zone, where collagen type IV and VII deposition is impaired
questions.exp: FDH is fundamentally a mesoectodermal dysplasia with the primary structural defect in the dermis. The PORCN protein regulates Wnt signaling, which is essential for normal dermal connective tissue development. Absence of normal Wnt signaling causes profound dermal thinning, allowing subcutaneous fat to herniate upward and directly abut the thinned epidermis, creating the characteristic cribriform atrophy pattern.
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: The DERMAL layer is the DESERT in the castle—PORCN is the water-carrier (Wnt pathway) that normally fills the dermal moat. Without it, the moat dries completely, the subcutaneous fat BULGES UP through the empty space like a beach ball in a deflated pool.

questions.q: A 3-day-old neonate presents with flaccid bullae on the buttocks and perineal area that rupture within 24-48 hours, leaving thin golden-yellow crusts with a characteristic peripheral collarette of scale. Nikolsky sign is negative and mucous membranes are spared. What is the primary target antigen cleaved by the staphylococcal exfoliative toxins in this condition?
opts: Desmoglein 3 (Dsg3)
Desmoglein 1 (Dsg1)
Desmoplakin I and II
E-cadherin
questions.exp: Bullous impetigo of the newborn is mediated by staphylococcal exfoliative toxins that specifically cleave desmoglein 1 (Dsg1), a desmosomal cadherin responsible for keratinocyte cell-to-cell adhesion in the superficial epidermis. The resulting intraepidermal split occurs beneath the stratum granulosum. The most common toxins are ETA (phage-encoded) and ETB (plasmid-encoded), produced by phage group II S. aureus (types 71 and 55).
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: Picture Dsg1 as a CASTLE BRIDGE (1) spanning the GRANULAR FLOOR—when the Staph KNIGHTS release their EXFOLIATIVE TOXINS (shaped like cleaver swords), they CUT the bridge between the GOLDEN (golden crust) STONE BLOCKS, leaving a GORGEOUS COLLAR (collarette) of the broken roof around the edge.

questions.q: A 24-year-old male presents with recurrent superficial peeling of the palms during summer months. Physical examination reveals discrete areas of skin peeling with small air-filled pockets that rupture centrally, leaving ragged rims of scale. The patient denies pruritus, pain, or inflammatory symptoms. Which histopathological finding is characteristic of keratolysis exfoliativa?
opts: Cleavage within the stratum corneum with premature corneocyte separation and partially degraded corneodesmosomes
Prominent inflammatory infiltrate with eosinophils and lymphocytes in the dermis
Acanthosis with hyperkeratosis and parakeratosis extending through multiple epidermal layers
Subepidermal bulla formation with full-thickness epidermolysis
questions.exp: Keratolysis exfoliativa shows characteristic histological cleavage within the stratum corneum due to premature separation of corneocytes from each other, with electron microscopy revealing partially degraded corneodesmosomes. The condition is notably non-inflammatory with no inflammatory infiltrate present. This distinction from bullous disorders and inflammatory dermatoses is crucial for diagnosis.

questions.q: A 5-year-old child develops a morbilliform rash that begins behind the ears and on the forehead, then spreads to the neck and trunk over the next 3 days. Which of the following best describes the temporal-spatial progression of the measles exanthem?
opts: Centripetal distribution starting from the trunk and spreading outward to extremities
Centrifugal distribution with simultaneous eruption across all body surfaces
Cephalocaudal (head-to-toe) direction, fading in the reverse order of appearance
Random distribution with predilection for flexural surfaces and coalescence on the palms
questions.exp:
The measles exanthem follows a strict cephalocaudal (head-to-toe) progression, beginning behind the ears, on the forehead, and at the anterior hairline, then spreading over 2–4 days to the neck, trunk, and extremities with coalescence on the face and neck. Importantly, the rash fades in the exact order it appeared, leaving coppery-brown discoloration and fine desquamation. This orderly progression is a key diagnostic feature distinguishing measles from other viral exanthems.
🏰 Palace: Imagine a MEASLES WAVE starting at the HEAD OFFICE (ears/forehead), cascading DOWN a staircase like a CEO walking floor-by-floor (cephalocaudal = head-down), then REVERSING up the stairs as it FADES—'CEPHALO' = captain's cabin at the top of the ship!

questions.q: A 3-year-old child presents with symmetric, monomorphic, flat-topped papules (2–4 mm) on the face, buttocks, and extensor surfaces of the arms and legs. Laboratory studies show elevated transaminases and negative HBsAg. Which of the following best explains this clinical presentation?
opts: Classic Gianotti-Crosti syndrome triggered by Hepatitis B surface antigen with concurrent anicteric hepatitis
Papulovesicular Acrolocated Syndrome (non-HBV associated), most likely triggered by Epstein-Barr virus or Coxsackievirus
Gianotti-Crosti syndrome exclusively affecting the palms and soles with mucosal involvement
Adult-onset Gianotti-Crosti syndrome with HLA-B27 predisposition
questions.exp: The patient's age (3 years), symmetric papular distribution on acral and facial sites with trunk sparing, combined with negative HBsAg and no mention of concurrent jaundice, is consistent with papulovesicular acrolocated syndrome, now the most common form due to routine HBV vaccination. EBV and Coxsackieviruses are the most frequent viral triggers in this non-HBV associated variant.

questions.q: A 4-year-old child presents with a unilateral pink-to-red morbilliform exanthem that began in the left axillary fold 3 days ago and is now spreading centrifugally across the ipsilateral trunk. Individual papules are surrounded by pale white halos. Which of the following best describes the primary pathological mechanism driving this condition?
opts: Th2-mediated allergic response to contact allergens
CD8+ cytotoxic T-lymphocyte-driven inflammatory response to viral antigens
IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation from food allergens
Type III immune complex deposition in dermal blood vessels
questions.exp: APEC/ULTE is a self-limiting paraviral exanthem with an inflammatory response driven primarily by CD8+ cytotoxic T-lymphocytes, despite the exact viral antigens or receptors being unknown. The pale white halos around papules and characteristic centrifugal spread from a unilateral flexural origin are hallmark clinical features of this CD8+ T-cell mediated condition.

questions.q: A newborn with a localized bullous impetigo has gram-positive cocci cultured from the blister fluid. On histopathology, which of the following findings would distinguish bullous impetigo from staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS)?
opts: Presence of subcorneal acantholytic blister
Dense inflammatory infiltrate of neutrophils within the blister cavity
Cleavage plane beneath the stratum granulosum
Systemic hematogenous spread of exfoliative toxins
questions.exp: Both bullous impetigo and SSSS feature a subcorneal acantholytic blister with cleavage beneath the stratum granulosum and target desmoglein 1. However, bullous impetigo is a localized infection with a dense neutrophilic inflammatory infiltrate within the blister cavity and upper dermis, and bacteria can be visualized and cultured directly from the fluid. In contrast, SSSS is a generalized toxin-mediated condition where exfoliative toxins act systemically from a distant focus with minimal local inflammation and no organisms in the bullae.
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: In the CASTLE DUNGEON, the LOCALIZED BULLOUS IMPETIGO room has ANGRY NEUTROPHIL GUARDS swarming everywhere (dense infiltrate + culturable bacteria), while the SSSS grand hall is eerily EMPTY of soldiers—only the GHOST of toxins floating through the air (systemic, no local inflammation, sterile bullae).

questions.q: A newborn girl has a small, flat vascular lesion on her forehead that was maximally sized at birth. By 6 months of age, the lesion is barely visible with only subtle skin atrophy remaining. By what age is involution typically complete in this type of congenital haemangioma?
opts: By 3–5 years of age
By 14 months of age
By 5–7 years of age
Never; the lesion persists indefinitely
questions.exp: Rapidly involuting congenital haemangiomas (RICH) begin regression within days to weeks after birth and are usually completely involuted by 14 months of age. Affected infants are frequently left with redundant, atrophic, and hypopigmented skin as residuum.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with a symmetric malar rash that worsens after sun exposure and is accompanied by systemic symptoms including arthralgia and fever. Histopathology shows interface dermatitis. According to Gilliam's classification, which category of cutaneous lupus erythematosus does this presentation represent?
opts: LE-nonspecific skin disease
LE-specific skin disease (Cutaneous Lupus Erythematosus)
Bullous LE
Intermittent Cutaneous Lupus Erythematosus
questions.exp: Gilliam's classification divides LE skin lesions into LE-specific (demonstrating characteristic interface dermatitis) and LE-nonspecific. The malar rash with interface dermatitis on histology is a hallmark feature of Acute Cutaneous Lupus Erythematosus (ACLE), which falls under LE-specific skin disease. The presence of interface dermatitis is the defining histopathologic feature that distinguishes LE-specific lesions from LE-nonspecific skin manifestations.
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: Picture the GILLIAM GATEWAY to the castle entrance—on one side stands the INTERFACE (dermatitis wall) marking the LE-SPECIFIC treasure rooms; on the other side lies the nonspecific courtyard. The MALAR RASH butterfly is perched on the INTERFACE wall, guiding you to the LE-specific door.

questions.q: A 45-year-old patient presents with acute onset of painful nodules and ulcerations on the lower extremities along with fever and neutrophilia. Histopathology shows a dense sterile neutrophilic infiltrate within the papillary and reticular dermis without vasculitis. Which classification category best describes this presentation?
opts: Primarily epidermal neutrophilic dermatosis
Primarily dermal neutrophilic dermatosis
Primarily subcutaneous and appendageal neutrophilic dermatosis
Primarily vascular neutrophilic dermatosis
questions.exp: The dense neutrophilic infiltrate involving the papillary and reticular dermis, combined with the clinical presentation of nodules, ulcerations, and systemic symptoms, is characteristic of primarily dermal neutrophilic dermatoses—particularly Sweet's syndrome (acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis) or pyoderma gangrenosum. The anatomic depth of the infiltrate is the primary basis for classification in neutrophilic dermatoses.

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman presents with a localized exanthem restricted to the medial anterior chest with scarlatiniform papules. Her presentation differs significantly from the typical childhood APEC presentation. This variant is most consistent with which subtype?
opts: Classic APEC/Unilateral Laterothoracic Exanthem (ULTE)
Unilateral Mediothoracic Exanthem (UMTE)
Superimposed Lateralized Exanthem of Childhood (SLEC)
Symmetrical Eruptive Exanthem of Adults (SEEA)
questions.exp: UMTE is the variant typically seen in adults and is distinguished by its highly restricted distribution localized specifically to the medial anterior chest, rather than the classic axillary or lateral thoracic regions seen in childhood APEC. The adult age and medial chest location are the key diagnostic clues for UMTE.

questions.q: A 6-year-old unvaccinated child presents with a 3-day history of high fever, coryza, conjunctivitis, and a barking cough. On intraoral examination, you note small bright red macules with blue-white centers on the buccal mucosa opposite the premolar teeth. What is the name of this characteristic enanthem?
opts: Warthin-Finkeldey cells
Koplik's spots
Hutchinson's spots
Forchheimer spots
questions.exp:
Koplik's spots are the pathognomonic enanthem of measles, appearing as tiny bright red macules with 1–2 mm blue-white ('grains of sand') centers on the buccal mucosa, typically opposite the premolar teeth. They appear 48 hours before the characteristic morbilliform exanthem and are diagnostic for measles during the prodromal phase. Warthin-Finkeldey cells are multinucleated giant cells found in lymph nodes and lymphoid tissues, not visible on mucosal examination.
🏰 Palace: Picture a KOPECK (coin) with a BLUE HALO sitting in a DENTAL CHAIR opposite premolars—'KOP-lik' sounds like a dental appointment where you spot the SAND in a MOUTH GRAIN shop!

questions.q: A dermatology resident encounters a case of keratolysis exfoliativa and reviews the proposed pathophysiological mechanism. Which of the following best describes the main pathological process leading to exfoliation in this condition?
opts: Premature corneodesmolysis from horizontal movement and decomposition of horny layer intercellular lipids by lipases, along with protease activity disrupting keratinocyte adhesion
Autoimmune destruction of hemidesmosomes at the dermal-epidermal junction
Genetic filaggrin mutations leading to impaired epidermal barrier function
Fungal colonization of the stratum corneum causing enzymatic degradation
questions.exp: Recent pathophysiological studies suggest that premature corneodesmolysis is the main mechanism, where intercellular lipids in the horny layer decompose due to lipases and steroid sulfatases, and proteases from the upper skin surface gradually disrupt keratinocyte adhesion. Notably, no genetic abnormalities including filaggrin mutations have been associated with this acquired disorder.

questions.q: Which of the following neutrophilic dermatoses is specifically characterized by infiltrates localized to the eccrine sweat glands and is frequently observed as a cutaneous adverse effect?
opts: Subcorneal pustular dermatosis
Pyoderma gangrenosum
Neutrophilic eccrine hidradenitis
Intraepidermal neutrophilic IgA dermatosis
questions.exp: Neutrophilic eccrine hidradenitis is a subcutaneous and appendageal neutrophilic dermatosis that targets eccrine sweat glands and is commonly seen in patients undergoing chemotherapy as a drug-related adverse effect. This condition differs from epidermal and dermal forms by virtue of its deeper, appendage-specific localization.
